Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$\varnothing\ne\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, and let $G$ be a finite group
([[def-group]]) acting on $\mathcal X$ by a left action
([[def-group-action]]). Require that each map $x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is
measurable from $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to itself and that
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For $\theta\in\Theta_0$, the null law is **invariant under the action** when
$P_\theta(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P_\theta(A)$ for every $g\in G$ and
$A\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, $g\cdot X$ and $X$ have the same law when
$X\sim P_\theta$. The setup defines the action and score whether or not this
invariance condition holds; the validity theorem below assumes it for every
null parameter.

The data space need not be finite, and the action need not be free. Group
elements, including distinct elements that send $x$ to the same point, remain
distinct transformations in every group average. On a finite data space with
the full power-set sigma-algebra, the setup specializes to
[[def-finite-group-randomization-test]].

In a setup as in [[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], the
**inclusive full-orbit upper-tail p-value** at $x\in\mathcal X$ is
$$p_{\mathrm{orb}}(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the data and uniform on $[0,1]$, meaning
$\mathbb P(U\le u)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized full-orbit
p-value** is
$$p_{\mathrm{tie}}(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Independence is in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]]. Each count is over group elements with
multiplicity, so nonfree actions are handled without replacing $|G|$ by the
number of distinct orbit points.

On the finite-space special case, these formulas are the inclusive and
tie-randomized ranks of [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]]. The null-law validity
argument is supplied separately from this definition.

Let $a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb R$ with $m\ge1$. Let $J$ be uniform on $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and let $U$ be independent of $J$ and uniform on $[0,1]$. Set
$$R_0:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i\ge a_J\}}{m},\qquad R_U:=\frac{\#\{i:a_i>a_J\}+U\#\{i:a_i=a_J\}}{m}.$$
Then $R_U$ is uniform on $[0,1]$, while $R_0$ is superuniform: $P(R_0\le u)\le u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty finite set. Its **uniform probability space** assigns every $\omega\in\Omega$ the weight $1/|\Omega|$. Thus every event $A\subseteq\Omega$ has
$$\mathbb P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.$$
Nonemptiness is required so that the denominator is positive.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

Let $p$ be a valid p-value for a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0$ in a
statistical experiment. For every $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the deterministic test
with rejection function
$$\varphi_\alpha(x)=\mathbf 1_{\{p(x)\le\alpha\}}$$
satisfies
$$P_\theta(p(X)\le\alpha)=E_\theta[\varphi_\alpha(X)]\le\alpha \qquad(\theta\in\Theta_0).$$
Consequently, whenever a nonempty alternative hypothesis
$\Theta_1\subseteq\Theta\setminus\Theta_0$ is specified, this test has size
at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$ in the sense of
[[def-test-size-and-power]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ be a measurable **action space**: a set of available
actions equipped with a sigma-algebra of action events, hence a measurable
space ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **randomized procedure** (or
randomized decision rule) is a probability kernel $K$ from
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, in the pointwise sense
of [[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]. Thus $K(x,\cdot)$ is a
probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$ for every $x\in\mathcal X$,
and $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable for every $B\in\mathcal G$.

action in $B$. The kernel is specified without reference to the unknown
parameter. This definition imposes no measurable structure on $\Theta$. The
kernel is the specification of the procedure; no representation by a separate
random seed is asserted for arbitrary measurable action spaces.

whose action set is $\{0,1\}$, equipped with its full sigma-algebra

[[def-sigma-algebra]]), where $1$ means reject and $0$ means do not reject
([[def-randomized-procedure-as-a-markov-kernel]]). Its **test function** is
$$\varphi(x)=K(x,\{1\}),\qquad x\in\mathcal X.$$
Since $K(x,\cdot)$ is a probability measure and $\{0\},\{1\}$ partition the
action set, $K(x,\{0\})+K(x,\{1\})=1$. Thus $\varphi(x)\in[0,1]$ and
$1-\varphi(x)=K(x,\{0\})$ is the probability of not rejecting. Give $[0,1]$
the trace of the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,+\infty]$, namely
$\{C\cap[0,1]:C\in\mathcal B([0,+\infty])\}$. By
[[lem-procedure-action-law-is-measurable]], $x\mapsto K(x,\{1\})$ is
measurable; since it has range in $[0,1]$, its preimage of $C\cap[0,1]$ equals
its preimage of $C$ and is measurable for every such $C$. Hence $\varphi$ is a
measurable map in the preimage sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Its value is the
rejection probability after observing $x$.
The convention $1=\text{reject}$ is fixed here. No null or alternative
hypothesis is part of this definition.

Let $\mathsf E=((X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a
statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]) and let
$\varphi:X\to[0,1]$ be measurable, where $[0,1]$ has its Borel sigma-algebra.
On the binary action space $\{0,1\}$ with its full sigma-algebra, define
$$K(x,B)=\varphi(x)\mathbf 1_B(1)+(1-\varphi(x))\mathbf 1_B(0)\qquad (B\subseteq\{0,1\}).$$
Then $K$ is a probability kernel and hence a randomized procedure; its
randomized-test function under the convention $1=\mathrm{reject}$ is
$\varphi$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Let
$\Theta_0,\Theta_1$ be nonempty disjoint subsets of $\Theta$, called the null
and alternative hypotheses. A hypothesis is **simple** when it is a singleton
and **composite** when it has at least two elements.

For a randomized test with test function
$\varphi:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$ ([[def-randomized-test]]), its **power function**
is
$$\beta(\theta):=E_\theta[\varphi(X)]\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
Its **size** is
$$\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\beta(\theta),$$
and it has **level $\alpha$** when this supremum is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. The expectations exist and lie in $[0,1]$ because
$0\le\varphi\le1$ and each $P_\theta$ is a probability measure
([[def-probability-measure]],
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]).
The supremum exists because $\Theta_0$ is nonempty, the values lie in
$[0,1]$, and $\mathbb R$ has the least-upper-bound property
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

derivations.claim: For each $g\in G$, $x\mapsto T(g\cdot x)$ is measurable by [F1]. For measurable real functions $f,h$, $\{f>h\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}\{f>q\}\cap\{h<q\}$, so strict comparisons are measurable; equality sets are complements of the union of the two opposite strict comparisons. Finite sums show that both rank counts are measurable. The identity belongs to $G$, so the tied count is at least one and both p-value formulas take values in $[0,1]$. For the joint tie-rank formula, partition the data space by the finitely many possible integer pairs $(N_>,N_=)$; on each part it is an affine function of $U$, so it is jointly measurable.

Fix $\theta\in\Theta_0$ and let $H$ be uniform on $G$, independent of $(X,U)$. For each fixed $h\in G$, invariance gives $h\cdot X\overset d=X$. Averaging over the finite law of $H$ therefore gives $(H\cdot X,U)\overset d=(X,U)$, so replacing $X$ by $H\cdot X$ does not change either p-value distribution.

Fix $x$ and form the finite list $a_g=T(g\cdot x)$ indexed by $g\in G$, retaining repeated values and repeated orbit points. At $H=h$, the transformed list at $h\cdot x$ is $T((gh)\cdot x)$ as $g$ ranges over $G$. Right multiplication $g\mapsto gh$ is a bijection of $G$, and the observed value $T(h\cdot x)$ is the entry indexed by $h$. Thus $p_{\mathrm{orb}}(h\cdot x)$ is the inclusive upper rank of a uniform index in $(a_g)_{g\in G}$, while $p_{\mathrm{tie}}(h\cdot x,U)$ is its independently tie-randomized rank.

By [F3], conditional on each fixed $x$, the first rank in step 2.1 is superuniform and the second is uniform. Averaging over $X$ preserves these bounds. The distributional equality in step 1.2 transfers them from $H\cdot X$ back to $X$, proving both displayed claims for this $\theta$. Since $\theta$ was arbitrary in $\Theta_0$, the claims hold under every null law. No orbit quotient or freeness assumption is used.

By [F6], $p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ is a valid p-value; [F7] gives its level-$\alpha$ cutoff test when an alternative is specified. For the tied test put $N_>(x)=\#\{g:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}$ and $N_=(x)=\#\{g:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}$. Its conditional rejection probability is $\phi_\alpha(x)=\min\{1,\max\{0,(|G|\alpha-N_>(x))/N_=(x)\}\}$, because $p_{\mathrm{tie}}(x,U)\le\alpha$ exactly when $U\le(|G|\alpha-N_>(x))/N_=(x)$, with the threshold clipped to $[0,1]$. The counts are measurable by step 1.1 and $N_=(x)\ge1$, so [F8] makes $\phi_\alpha$ a randomized test. Its null rejection probability equals $\mathbb P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{tie}}(X,U)\le\alpha)=\alpha$ by step 3.1, and [F9] identifies its size as $\alpha$ when a nonempty disjoint alternative is specified. The argument uses only a finite uniform group index and the stated uniform tie randomizer; it uses no choice axiom.

([[def-complete-ordered-field]]).

For the binary action $a\in\{0,1\}$, where $1$ means reject, the
**zero-one error loss** is $1$ when $a=1$ and $\theta\in\Theta_0$, or when
$a=0$ and $\theta\in\Theta_1$, and is $0$ otherwise. The decision-rule risk
from [[def-loss-function-and-risk]] integrates this loss against the action
kernel and data law. For each fixed $\theta$, its section on the binary
action space is measurable. The risk identities proved in
[[lem-test-zero-one-loss-risk-identities]] show that risk equals
$\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_0$ and $1-\beta(\theta)$ on $\Theta_1$. Thus size
is the worst null error risk, and power is the rejection probability under
each alternative parameter.

An **experiment** is a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, a set $\Theta$ of
parameter labels, and a family $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of probability
measures on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ ([[def-measurable-space]],
[[def-probability-measure]]). The measures $P_\theta$ are the sampling laws.
If data under a parameter value are realized as a random element, its law is
the pushforward measure $P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B))$ from
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]; it is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]].

The definition specifies the family of laws only. It supplies no sigma-algebra
on $\Theta$, no measurability condition on $\theta\mapsto P_\theta$, and no
common underlying probability space on which all observations must be realized.

derivations.claim: For the selected design, $\mathcal W$ is finite. Every $A\in\mathcal A\otimes2^{\mathcal W}$ has measurable sections $A_w=\{x:(x,w)\in A\}$. The displayed finite sum $\widetilde P_\theta(A)=\sum_w\nu(w)P_\theta(A_w)$ is nonnegative with total mass one. For disjoint $A_n$, each section $(\bigcup_nA_n)_w$ is the disjoint union of $(A_n)_w$, so countable additivity of $P_\theta$ and the finite sum over $w$ give countable additivity of $\widetilde P_\theta$. Thus [F11] makes this a joint statistical experiment. For measurable real functions $f,h$, $\{f\ge h\}$ is measurable because $\{f<h\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}\{f<q\}\cap\{h>q\}$. Therefore each section $x\mapsto p_B(x,w)$ is measurable. Since $\mathcal W$ is finite, each sublevel set of $p_B$ is a finite union of measurable sections $A_w\times\{w\}$, so $p_B$ is measurable on the joint space. The distinguished identity contributes one tied-or-higher value, so $1/(B+1)\le p_B\le1$; at $B=0$, $W=\{e\}$ and $p_B=1$.

First use the with-replacement design. Represent $W$ by its $B+1$ generating positions to choose an independent uniform position $J$, and write $H$ for the entry at that position. The unordered multiset $WH^{-1}$ has the same law as $W$: if $J$ is the identity position it is unchanged; if $J=j>0$, right multiplication by $H^{-1}=g_j^{-1}$ makes position $j$ equal to $e$, makes the former identity position $g_j^{-1}$ uniform on $G$, and leaves the other $B-1$ draws conditionally independent uniform on $G$. Thus, after order is ignored, there is again one distinguished identity and $B$ IID uniform group elements.

Now use the without-replacement design and put $w=B+1$. The possible sets $W$ are the $w$-element subsets of $G$ containing $e$, all equally likely. Given $W$, choose $H$ uniformly from its $w$ elements. The map $(W,H)\mapsto(WH^{-1},H)$ is a bijection from pairs with $e\in W$, $|W|=w$, $H\in W$ onto pairs $(S,h)$ with $e\in S$, $|S|=w$, $h^{-1}\in S$: its inverse is $(S,h)\mapsto(Sh,h)$. Each fixed $S$ in the image has exactly $w$ possible $h$, so $WH^{-1}$ has the same uniform-subset law as $W$.

Since $X$ is independent of $(W,J)$ and each fixed $H\in G$ preserves its null law, conditioning on $(W,J)$ gives $H\cdot X\overset d=X$. By step 1.2, $WH^{-1}$ has the same design law as $W$, so $(H\cdot X,WH^{-1})$ and $(X,W)$ have the same joint law. Now fix $x$ and a labelled presentation of a with-replacement multiset $W$ before drawing $J$. The value $p_B(H\cdot x,WH^{-1})$ counts, with multiplicity, the entries $w\in W$ for which $T(w\cdot x)\ge T(H\cdot x)$, because $(wH^{-1})\cdot(H\cdot x)=w\cdot x$. As $J$ is uniform over the $B+1$ positions, this is the inclusive upper rank of a uniform position in the score multiset $(T(w\cdot x))_{w\in W}$. By [F5] this rank is superuniform conditional on $x,W$; averaging and using the joint-law equality transfers the bound to $p_B(X,W)$. This proves the with-replacement case, with ties and duplicate transformations counted by position.

The auxiliary pair $(W,H)$ is independent of $X$. For each fixed value of that pair, invariance gives $H\cdot X\overset d=X$; step 1.3 gives $WH^{-1}$ the same design law as $W$. Hence $(H\cdot X,WH^{-1})$ and $(X,W)$ have the same joint law. To bound the transformed p-value, fix $x,W$ before drawing $H$. Conditional on $W$, $H$ is uniform over its $B+1$ elements, and $p_B(H\cdot x,WH^{-1})$ is the inclusive upper rank of that selected position in $(T(g\cdot x))_{g\in W}$, since $(gH^{-1})\cdot(H\cdot x)=g\cdot x$. Thus, when a nonempty disjoint alternative is specified, [F10] gives size at most $\alpha$ and hence level $\alpha$. Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$\varnothing\ne\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, and let $G$ be a finite group
([[def-group]]) acting on $\mathcal X$ by a left action
([[def-group-action]]). Require that each map $x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is
measurable from $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to itself and that
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For $\theta\in\Theta_0$, the null law is **invariant under the action** when
$P_\theta(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P_\theta(A)$ for every $g\in G$ and
$A\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, $g\cdot X$ and $X$ have the same law when
$X\sim P_\theta$. The setup defines the action and score whether or not this
invariance condition holds; the validity theorem below assumes it for every
null parameter.

The data space need not be finite, and the action need not be free. Group
elements, including distinct elements that send $x$ to the same point, remain
distinct transformations in every group average. On a finite data space with
the full power-set sigma-algebra, the setup specializes to
[[def-finite-group-randomization-test]].

In a setup as in [[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], the
**inclusive full-orbit upper-tail p-value** at $x\in\mathcal X$ is
$$p_{\mathrm{orb}}(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the data and uniform on $[0,1]$, meaning
$\mathbb P(U\le u)=u$ for every $u\in[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized full-orbit
p-value** is
$$p_{\mathrm{tie}}(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Independence is in the sense of
[[def-independent-random-elements]]. Each count is over group elements with
multiplicity, so nonfree actions are handled without replacing $|G|$ by the
number of distinct orbit points.

On the finite-space special case, these formulas are the inclusive and
tie-randomized ranks of [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]]. The null-law validity
argument is supplied separately from this definition.

Let $\mathsf E,\Theta_0,G,T$ be as in
[[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], and suppose every null law
$P_\theta$, $\theta\in\Theta_0$, is invariant under the action. Let
$p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{tie}}$ be as in
[[def-measurable-finite-group-orbit-pvalues]]. Then, for every
$u\in[0,1]$ and every $\theta\in\Theta_0$,
$$P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{orb}}(X)\le u)\le u,\qquad \mathbb P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{tie}}(X,U)\le u)=u,$$
where $U$ is independent uniform on $[0,1]$. Thus $p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ is a
valid p-value; its cutoff has null rejection probability at most $\alpha$,
and hence size at most $\alpha$ when a nonempty disjoint alternative is
specified. The tie-randomized cutoff is a randomized test with rejection
probability exactly $\alpha$ under each null law. These level and size
statements use [[def-test-size-and-power]].

On finite sample spaces, the first two distributional claims specialize to
[[thm-finite-group-randomization-validity]] and use the same multiplicity
convention as [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]]. The proof below supplies the
measurable-space extension rather than importing it from that finite-space
supplier.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

**Input:** a measurable finite-group setup
[[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], an observed $x$, an
integer $B\ge0$, and one of the two simulation designs below. Simulated
transformations are independent of $X$.

1. **With replacement.** Draw $g_1,\ldots,g_B$ independently and uniformly
   from $G$. Set $g_0=e$, the identity, and return
   $$\widehat p_{B,\mathrm{wr}}(x):=\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbf 1\{T(g_b\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{B+1}.$$
   A simulated draw may itself equal $e$; it is still counted in addition to
   the distinguished identity.
2. **Without replacement.** Require $B\le |G|-1$. Draw a subset $S$ uniformly
   from the $B$-element subsets of $G\setminus\{e\}$, and return
   $$\widehat p_{B,\mathrm{wor}}(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in\{e\}\cup S:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{B+1}.$$
   This is a uniform-subset design; the selected transformations are distinct
   and the identity is adjoined.

In either design, a cutoff rule rejects when the returned value is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. For $B=0$ the only transformation is the distinguished
identity and the returned value is $1$. Validity under an invariant null law,
including ties, is a separate theorem on this page.

derivations.claim: All four masses are nonnegative and sum to $(q+(1-q))^2=1$, so [F4] makes them a finite probability law. The swap fixes $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$ and exchanges $(0,1)$ with $(1,0)$, which have equal mass. Thus $P_q(s^{-1}A)=P_q(A)$ for every $A\subseteq\Omega$, and the group action is invariant for every $q\in[0,1]$.

The subset $S$ is uniform and independent of $X$ by the Example, so it satisfies the without-replacement design premise in [F5]. In the $\mathbb Z/6\mathbb Z$ example, addition by any fixed group element permutes the six equally likely outcomes, so the null law is invariant. If $X=0$, only the identity in $W$ has score at least $T(X)=1$, and the without-replacement p-value is $1/3$. If $X\ne0$, then $T(X)=0$ and every element of $W$ has score at least zero, so the p-value is $1$. Its distribution is therefore $1/3$ with probability $1/6$ and $1$ with probability $5/6$; its CDF is superuniform.

At $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$, both transformed scores are $0$, giving $p_{\mathrm{orb}}=1$ and $p_{\mathrm{tie}}=U$. At $(1,0)$ the two scores are $1,-1$, giving $p_{\mathrm{orb}}=1/2$ and $p_{\mathrm{tie}}=U/2$. At $(0,1)$ they are $-1,1$, giving $p_{\mathrm{orb}}=1$ and $p_{\mathrm{tie}}=(1+U)/2$.

Put $a=q(1-q)$. Then $p_{\mathrm{orb}}=1/2$ with probability $a$ and equals $1$ otherwise. Its CDF is $0$ for $u<1/2$, $a\le1/4\le u$ for $1/2\le u<1$, and $1$ at $u=1$, so it is superuniform. For $0\le u\le1/2$, the tie-randomized CDF is $2au+(1-2a)u=u$: the $(1,0)$ branch contributes $2au$, the $(0,1)$ branch contributes zero except at a probability-zero endpoint, and the tied branches contribute $(1-2a)u$. For $1/2\le u\le1$, it is $a+a(2u-1)+(1-2a)u=u$. Thus $p_{\mathrm{tie}}$ is uniform, in agreement with [F3].

In the weak mean-difference example, $E[X]=E[Y]=0$. But the coordinate swap sends $(1,0)$ to $(0,1)$, and the product law assigns these points probabilities $P(X=1)Q(Y=0)=1/4$ and $P(X=0)Q(Y=1)=0$, respectively. Hence this weak null does not make the pooled law invariant under the swap, so the invariant-null premise of [F3] cannot be inferred from equality of means.

Let $N\ge1$, and let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ index the fixed
experimental units at the actual treatment-assignment level. Let
$\mathcal Z$ be a nonempty finite set of allowed assignments. If treatment
is assigned to clusters, each cluster is one indexed unit; no separate
probability-sampling unit is present. The index $i$ identifies that unit,
and no visit or repeated-measurement index is modeled here.

A known assignment law is a function $p:\mathcal Z\to[0,1]$ satisfying
$\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)=1$, so $(\mathcal Z,p)$ is a finite probability
space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]); assignments of probability
zero may remain in $\mathcal Z$. A **potential-outcome schedule** is a function
$\theta:\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$, with
$Y_i(z):=\theta(i,z)$. The schedule and the units are fixed; the assignment
$Z$ is the only randomness supplied by the design, and the observed response
vector is $Y_\theta(Z)=(Y_i(Z))_{i\in\mathcal I}$. The schedule is defined
for every allowed assignment, including zero-probability assignments, and
may depend on the full assignment vector, so no no-interference assumption is
implicit. The scientific statistical model contract
[[def-scientific-statistical-model-contract]] requires the observation space,
units, quantity status, observation mechanism, support, conditioning
convention, and adequacy assumptions to be recorded; this model specifies
those fields as follows.

To express this as a statistical experiment, take the data space
$\mathcal X=\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}$ with its full power-set
sigma-algebra, which is a sigma-algebra by [[def-sigma-algebra]] and makes
$\mathcal X$ a measurable space ([[def-measurable-space]]), and parameter
set $\Theta=\mathbb R^{\mathcal I\times\mathcal Z}$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$
let $P_\theta$ be the law
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]) of the deterministic
observation map $O_\theta(z)=(z,Y_\theta(z))$ from $(\mathcal Z,p)$. The map
is measurable because its domain has the full power set, in the preimage
sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]], and its law
is a probability measure by
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]. Thus
$((\mathcal X,2^{\mathcal X}),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$ is an
experiment in the sense of [[def-statistical-experiment]]. The assignment
law asserts no response-error model, Gaussian law, superpopulation
randomization, or sampling representativeness beyond the stated finite
assignment mechanism. Its finite full-measure support set is
$$S_\theta:=\{(z,Y_\theta(z)):z\in\mathcal Z,\ p(z)>0\},$$
since $P_\theta(S_\theta)=\sum_{z:p(z)>0}p(z)=1$. The record contains the
assigned vector and every unit's response; missing or censored outcomes and
repeated visits require a separately declared observation mechanism. The
inferential target is the assignment-invariance hypothesis for these $N$
units, not an estimand for a wider population.

Inference in this page holds $\mathcal I$ and $\theta$ fixed and averages
over the declared law $p$; it does not condition on the realized assignment.
The status of the quantities is explicit: $\theta$ and all
$Y_i(z)$ are fixed, $Z$ is random, $(Z,Y_\theta(Z))$ is observed, and
potential responses under unassigned vectors are fixed but latent. The
assignment set, weights, and implemented randomization protocol are
design-controlled and should be checked against protocol records. Assignment
logs and response records are empirically assessable, but those checks do not
prove that the declared law generated the data. Potential outcomes under
unassigned vectors are fixed and latent in the realized record. This does
not imply nonidentifiability from the observed-data law: for each $z$ with
$p(z)>0$, the law assigns mass $p(z)$ to $(z,Y_\theta(z))$, and therefore
determines $Y_\theta(z)$. Assignment invariance on this positive-probability
set is **empirically assessable**, and the theorem tests the stronger
invariance hypothesis on all allowed assignments. Values at assignments
with $p(z)=0$, and restrictions on those values, are **substantively
untestable** from this law, since changing them leaves $P_\theta$ unchanged.
One realized assignment does not reveal responses at other assignments.
These classifications do not make the design or scientific model
empirically true.

In the finite randomized treatment-assignment model
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]], a schedule satisfies
the **Fisher sharp null** when for each unit $i$ there is a value $y_i$ such that
$Y_i(z)=y_i$ for every allowed assignment $z$. The full vector
$y=(y_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}$ is then imputable under every assignment.

A **predeclared ordering score** is a real-valued statistic
$T:\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R^{\mathcal I}\to\mathbb R$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]) fixed before the
assignment and outcomes are inspected. Its upper-tail ordering includes ties:
assignment $z'$ is at least as extreme as $z$ when $T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)$.
For a signed score $S$ and fixed null center $s_0$, the corresponding
two-sided ordering is explicitly $T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$. The center is part
of the predeclared ordering; the sharp null alone does not force $s_0=0$
for an arbitrary signed score. A lower-tail ordering is represented by
using $-S$ as the score. A statistic in this setting is a measurable map in
the sense of [[def-statistic-and-estimator]]; the full power-set data
sigma-algebra makes every such real-valued map measurable.

In a finite randomized treatment-assignment model, fix any real-valued
predeclared ordering score $T(z,y)$. For observed data $(z,y)$ define
$$p_{\rm rand}(z,y):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)\ge T(z,y)\}.$$
Let $\lambda$ be the uniform probability measure on the Borel subsets of
$[0,1]$. For each $\theta$, equip $\mathcal X\times[0,1]$ with the product
sigma-algebra $2^{\mathcal X}\otimes\mathcal B([0,1])$ and define
$$\widetilde P_\theta(E):=\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)\,\lambda\bigl(\{u\in[0,1]:((z,Y_\theta(z)),u)\in E\}\bigr).$$
Let $U$ be the $[0,1]$ coordinate on this extension. Define
$$p^+(z,y,U):=\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)>T(z,y)\}+U\sum_{z'\in\mathcal Z}p(z')1\{T(z',y)=T(z,y)\}.$$
For every schedule satisfying the Fisher sharp null and every
$u\in[0,1]$,
$$P_\theta\!\left(p_{\rm rand}(Z,Y_\theta(Z))\le u\right)\le u,$$
whereas the added randomization gives
$$\widetilde P_\theta\!\left(p^+(Z,Y_\theta(Z),U)\le u\right)=u.$$

and randomized ties give an exactly uniform p-value when the additional
independent uniform randomizer is used. For a two-sided test, take
$T(z,y)=|S(z,y)-s_0|$ with its center $s_0$ fixed in advance. The result
uses the actual, possibly unequal assignment probabilities; random
assignment supplies no Gaussian error law, and this theorem makes no
validity claim under the weak zero-average-effect null from
[[def-finite-population-average-treatment-effect-and-weak-null]] unless it
is also Fisher-sharp.

Let $\mathsf E,\Theta_0,G,T$ be as in
[[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], and suppose every null law
$P_\theta$, $\theta\in\Theta_0$, is invariant under the action. Let
$p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ and $p_{\mathrm{tie}}$ be as in
[[def-measurable-finite-group-orbit-pvalues]]. Then, for every
$u\in[0,1]$ and every $\theta\in\Theta_0$,
$$P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{orb}}(X)\le u)\le u,\qquad \mathbb P_\theta(p_{\mathrm{tie}}(X,U)\le u)=u,$$
where $U$ is independent uniform on $[0,1]$. Thus $p_{\mathrm{orb}}$ is a
valid p-value; its cutoff has null rejection probability at most $\alpha$,
and hence size at most $\alpha$ when a nonempty disjoint alternative is
specified. The tie-randomized cutoff is a randomized test with rejection
probability exactly $\alpha$ under each null law. These level and size
statements use [[def-test-size-and-power]].

On finite sample spaces, the first two distributional claims specialize to
[[thm-finite-group-randomization-validity]] and use the same multiplicity
convention as [[def-orbit-rank-p-value]]. The proof below supplies the
measurable-space extension rather than importing it from that finite-space
supplier.

Consider the no-interference binary-treatment submodel of
[[def-finite-randomized-treatment-assignment-model]] in which the allowed
assignment set is $\{0,1\}^{\mathcal I}$ and unit $i$'s response under
assignment vector $z$ is $Y_i(z)=Y_i(z_i)$ for fixed real potential responses
$Y_i(0)$ and $Y_i(1)$. For the fixed units, define the
**finite-population average treatment effect** by
$$\tau_F:=\frac1N\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\bigl(Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\bigr).$$
The **weak zero-average-effect null** is the hypothesis $\tau_F=0$; it
constrains the average of the unit-level effects, not each effect separately.
The Fisher sharp null in this submodel, defined in
[[def-fisher-sharp-null-and-predeclared-test-orderings]], requires
$Y_i(1)=Y_i(0)$ for every unit. No probability distribution on the fixed
potential responses is part of either definition.

derivations.claim: The assignment weights are nonnegative and sum to one. Under the sharp null the same fixed response vector $y$ is available at both assignments, so the two score values in the Example are imputable before observing $Z$. The published weighted randomization theorem [F3] therefore applies to this schedule and this predeclared ordering.
If $Z=a$, the only assignment with score at least $1$ is $a$, so $p_{\mathrm{rand}}(a,y)=0.9$. If $Z=b$, both assignments have score at least $0$, so $p_{\mathrm{rand}}(b,y)=0.9+0.1=1$.

The p-value is $0.9$ with probability $0.9$ and $1$ with probability $0.1$. Its CDF is $0$ for $u<0.9$, $0.9\le u$ for $0.9\le u<1$, and $1$ at $u=1$, hence it is superuniform. The assignment law is not invariant under the swap $a\leftrightarrow b$, since the two assignment masses differ, so the group-invariance theorem [F4] is not the justification here. This example uses the Fisher sharp null and makes no claim under the weaker average-effect null [F5].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]), let
$\varnothing\ne\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, and let $G$ be a finite group
([[def-group]]) acting on $\mathcal X$ by a left action
([[def-group-action]]). Require that each map $x\mapsto g\cdot x$ is
measurable from $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ to itself and that
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For $\theta\in\Theta_0$, the null law is **invariant under the action** when
$P_\theta(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P_\theta(A)$ for every $g\in G$ and
$A\in\mathcal A$. Equivalently, $g\cdot X$ and $X$ have the same law when
$X\sim P_\theta$. The setup defines the action and score whether or not this
invariance condition holds; the validity theorem below assumes it for every
null parameter.

The data space need not be finite, and the action need not be free. Group
elements, including distinct elements that send $x$ to the same point, remain
distinct transformations in every group average. On a finite data space with
the full power-set sigma-algebra, the setup specializes to
[[def-finite-group-randomization-test]].

**Input:** a measurable finite-group setup
[[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], an observed $x$, an
integer $B\ge0$, and one of the two simulation designs below. Simulated
transformations are independent of $X$.

1. **With replacement.** Draw $g_1,\ldots,g_B$ independently and uniformly
   from $G$. Set $g_0=e$, the identity, and return
   $$\widehat p_{B,\mathrm{wr}}(x):=\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbf 1\{T(g_b\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{B+1}.$$
   A simulated draw may itself equal $e$; it is still counted in addition to
   the distinguished identity.
2. **Without replacement.** Require $B\le |G|-1$. Draw a subset $S$ uniformly
   from the $B$-element subsets of $G\setminus\{e\}$, and return
   $$\widehat p_{B,\mathrm{wor}}(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in\{e\}\cup S:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{B+1}.$$
   This is a uniform-subset design; the selected transformations are distinct
   and the identity is adjoined.

In either design, a cutoff rule rejects when the returned value is at most
$\alpha\in[0,1]$. For $B=0$ the only transformation is the distinguished
identity and the returned value is $1$. Validity under an invariant null law,
including ties, is a separate theorem on this page.

In a setup as in [[def-measurable-finite-group-permutation-setup]], suppose
every null law is invariant. Fix $B\ge0$ and use either design of
[[alg-random-permutation-monte-carlo-pvalue]]. With replacement, let $W$ be
the unordered transformation multiset, with multiplicity, represented by
$(e,g_1,\ldots,g_B)$, where the $g_b$ are independent uniform draws from
$G$. Without replacement, let $W=\{e\}\cup S$,
where $S$ is a uniformly selected $B$-subset of $G\setminus\{e\}$ and
$B\le|G|-1$. In both cases define
$$p_B(X,W):=\frac{\#\{g\in W:T(g\cdot X)\ge T(X)\}}{B+1},$$
counting multiplicity in the with-replacement case.

Let $\mathcal W$ be the finite set of possible transformation multisets for
the with-replacement design or subsets for the without-replacement design,
and let $\nu$ be the induced design law. On $\mathcal X\times\mathcal W$ use the joint experiment whose law at
$\theta$ is
$$\widetilde P_\theta(A):=\sum_{w\in\mathcal W}\nu(w)\,P_\theta(\{x:(x,w)\in A\})$$
for $A$ in the product sigma-algebra. Then
$$\widetilde P_\theta(p_B(X,W)\le u)\le u\qquad(\theta\in\Theta_0,\ 0\le u\le1).$$
Thus $p_B$ is a valid p-value on the joint experiment and its cutoff has null
rejection probability at most $\alpha$. When a nonempty disjoint alternative
is specified, the cutoff test has size at most $\alpha$ and is level
$\alpha$. The proof treats the uniform-subset design separately; the
without-replacement formula is not inferred from the with-replacement case.
If $B=|G|-1$ without replacement, $W=G$ and the formula reduces to the
full-orbit value of [[thm-finite-group-permutation-validity]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **p-value
statistic** is a statistic $p:\mathcal X\to[0,1]$, where $[0,1]$ carries the
trace of the Borel sigma-algebra, meaning
$\{B\cap[0,1]:B\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\}$
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]).

For a nonempty null hypothesis $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$, the statistic is a
**valid p-value for $\Theta_0$** if it is superuniform under every null law:
$$P_\theta(\{x:p(x)\le u\})\le u\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta_0\text{ and }u\in[0,1].$$
The variable $p(X)$ is the observed p-value when the data are $X$. The
validity condition is distributional; measurability alone does not imply it.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty finite set. Its **uniform probability space** assigns every $\omega\in\Omega$ the weight $1/|\Omega|$. Thus every event $A\subseteq\Omega$ has
$$\mathbb P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.$$
Nonemptiness is required so that the denominator is positive.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Consequently $P(\widetilde p_1\le0)=1/4>0$, contradicting the necessary superuniform bound [F4]. Thus the uncorrected fraction can equal zero and is anti-conservative at cutoff $0$.

In the same witness the corrected value is $p_+=(1+\mathbf1\{T(g_1\cdot X)\ge T(X)\})/2$, so it equals $1/2$ with probability $1/4$ and $1$ with probability $3/4$. Its CDF is $0$ below $1/2$, $1/4\le u$ for $1/2\le u<1$, and $1$ at $u=1$, consistent with the general identity-corrected result [F3].
